evidence.label: All-temperature pressure for orthogonally invariant Ising spin glasses

headline: A formula for the pressure of orthogonally invariant Ising spin glasses holds at every temperature.
scope: It covers Ising spin glasses with randomly rotated eigenvectors and an eigenvalue spread that settles to a bounded shape, with no outliers.
plain: A spin glass is a model of many tiny magnets with random, conflicting pulls between pairs. Here the pulls come from a matrix with fixed eigenvalues and random directions. The paper proves a formula for the system's key summary number, the pressure, at every temperature. Earlier formulas only worked when the temperature was high.
doesNot: This does not cover eigenvalue spreads with outliers outside the limiting range.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Giorgio Parisi, hierarchical order parameter for spin glasses
scorecard.significanceWhy: It extends rigorous pressure formulas for invariant spin glasses from high temperature to every temperature.

explanation:
Take two tiny magnets, called spins, each pointing up (+1) or down (−1). Give the pair an energy reward of 1 when they agree and a penalty of 1 when they disagree. There are four ways to set the two spins. Two agree and two disagree. Weight each setting by e raised to its reward, so agreeing settings count e and disagreeing ones count 1/e. Average these four weights, take the log, and divide by the number of spins. The result is the pressure. Here it is ½ × log(cosh 1), about 0.217.

A spin glass does the same with N spins and random rewards between every pair. The pressure is the key number. It sums up the system's behavior at one temperature, and its limit as N grows is what physicists want. For the classic Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model, Parisi introduced a layered order parameter in 1979[11]. Guerra proved one half of it, and Talagrand proved the full formula in 2006[12,13].

The rewards form a matrix. A matrix has eigenvalues, which say how strongly it acts in certain directions, the eigenvectors. This paper studies orthogonally invariant spin glasses. You fix the eigenvalues and spin the eigenvectors to a completely random direction. The question is whether the eigenvalues alone fix the limiting pressure.

The obstacle is a mismatch. The eigenvalues describe the matrix on all of space. But spins only take the values ±1, the corners of a cube, so the matrix is only ever tested there[1]. Earlier rigorous formulas for these models needed high temperature[2]. Bhattacharya and Sen proved one such formula with no outside field[14]. At high temperature the spins behave simply and the hard structure never appears.

The paper proves a formula for the limiting pressure at every fixed temperature[3]. It assumes the spread of eigenvalues settles to a fixed shape on a bounded range. It also assumes the largest and smallest eigenvalues do not stray outside that range. The pressure converges on average, and also for almost every random draw, to a variational formula[4,5]. A variational formula is one given as the best value over a family of trial choices. The eigenvalue spread need not have a density or any minimum variance[7].

The formula keeps the layered overlap structure known from the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model[6]. Overlaps measure how alike two random samples of the spins are. The paper also handles outside fields acting on each spin[8]. By letting the temperature go to zero, it gets the lowest possible energy with no field[9]. One example is a Hopfield model built from a random Gaussian matrix. There the formula also gives the matrix's largest and smallest stretch over ±1 vectors[10].

The proof uses a tree-like overlap structure to describe all the overlaps at once[15]. The order of the minimum and maximum in the formula matters, and the proof never swaps them[16].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal versions of the main limits. They cover the pressure in expectation and almost surely, every positive temperature and the ground-state limit. They also cover outside fields, random spectra and the Gaussian-pattern case. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Solid if the proof holds. Lean has formal versions of the main limits; no specialist review is published.

The log of the averaged weight of all spin settings, divided by the number of spins.
Numbers saying how strongly a matrix stretches along its special directions, the eigenvectors.
